utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning, Your Honour. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. First of all, I would like to greet our witness. I'll ask him to take the solemn declaration later on. I would like to greet the Prosecution, and I'd like to ask the Prosecutor to introduce himself because I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, on behalf of the Prosecution I'd like to introduce both colleagues that are sitting with me today. Mr. Mathias Marcussen on my left who will be leading the witness and Mr. Calogero Ferrara who will be leading witnesses in subsequent proceedings in this case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Welcome to this -- to these proceedings to both of you. I would also like to greet Mr. Seselj and all those who assist us for this hearing and for future hearings. Before I ask the witness to take the solemn declaration, let me give you the following piece of information: Next week we are supposed to be sitting in the afternoon, but another courtroom is available and we'll be able to sit in the morning. Therefore, on Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday we'll be sitting in the morning. That's preferable, because everybody's in a better shape in the morning. Next week, therefore, we'll be working in the morning. That's what I wanted to say before we start, but now I'm going to ask the witness to stand up. Could you please give me your first name, last name, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Reynaud Theunens, Your Honour, and I'm born on the 2nd of January, 1965 in Brussels in Belgium.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your profession or your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm an intelligence analyst, military, in the Office of the Prosecutor at the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you testified before this Tribunal as an expert witness and if that's the case tell us in which cases.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I testified in the Milosevic trial in February 2004, in the Martic trial in February 2006, and in the trial known as the Vukovar 3 trial, the trial of Mr. Mrksic, Sljvancanin, Radic in June, July 2006.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've already testified three times.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question before I ask you to take the solemn declaration. You stated that you were a military analyst. So I suppose that before you came to work here in this Tribunal you served in the military. I would like to know if that is the case and in which units you served and with what rank.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. Actually, I'm still a member of the Belgian armed forces. I'm seconded to the ICTY which means that I am a UN servant but I still have my position in the Belgian military if I would like to return there. After my service at the military academy, I started my career as an officer first as a platoon commander and then as a deputy and first year's command in the military academy, and after that, so since 1992, I've been working as a military intelligence analyst in various positions in the Belgian Ministry of Defence. And, excuse me, I have the rank of in Belgian of captain commandant which is a rank between captain and major, OF-3 in the [indiscernible] we use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. We may have the opportunity to return to this during the examination-in-chief and during the cross-examination as well. Please read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated. Let me give you some information before I give the floor to the Prosecution. You've already testified three times. Therefore, what I say won't come as a surprise to you. You know that you will first have to answer questions put to you by the representative of the OTP as part of what we call the examination-in-chief. Five hours have been granted to the Prosecution for that purpose. Questions will be put to you, documents will be put to you as well, and you'll be answering the questions of the Prosecution. The three Judges sitting before you may at any time interrupt and ask you questions, ask you to expand on some answers or ask you to deal with matters that the Prosecution was not considering, and all this in the interest of justice. Following the examination-in-chief, the accused Mr. Seselj who is sitting on your left, the accused then will move on to the cross-examination. Mr. Seselj has been granted the same amount of time as the Prosecution, i.e., five hours. As you know, the cross-examination is made up of leading questions, and it can be quite an ordeal for a witness. Please do not be surprised at the way some questions may be put to you or at the tone that may be used when putting these questions to you, but the Judges will be there to control the proceedings. As you know, and I better say it straight away, the cross-examination has for its aim to test the credibility of the witness, and the second purpose of the cross-examination is to check that what the witness has stated in his answers to the Prosecution or in his report is accurate. So as I said, cross-examination can turn into quite an ordeal for an expert witness. Please try to be as accurate as possible when answering questions put to you, but you are a military man, so I'm not worried about the accuracy you will show when answering questions. If a question is unclear to you, do not hesitate to ask for the question to be rephrased even if the Judges have put that question to you, because some questions may be rather complex or lengthy and may be quite difficult to understand. So in that case do not hesitate to ask for the question to be rephrased. As you know, every hour and a half we take a break, a 20-minute break. If at any time during the proceedings you feel unwell tell us immediately. Then I'll interrupt the proceedings. And if at any time you want to address the Judges directly, please do so if you believe that your question may be useful. This is by way of an introduction in order for these proceedings to run as smoothly as possible in the interest of justice. Let me now give the floor to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Theunens, you said that you were a military analyst in the Office of the Prosecutor. What section do you work in?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I work in a team which is known as the Military Analysis Team, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And what does that team do?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: In the -- in the Military Analysis Team we have analysts who look at, in simple terms, at the military aspects of information that is relevant for the Office of the Prosecutor. In more concrete terms, we will study military structures, command and control, weapon systems, the interface between political authority and military command within the armed forces both from the de jure, so as it is foreseen in the legislation, as well as in the -- as well as from the de facto, i.e., how it was on the ground, point of view. And myself and some of my colleagues have already testified on these issues in other trials.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, you -- you've described briefly that you have served in the Belgian army. Could you -- could you describe in a little more detail your military service.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I said before, so after my studies in military academy and in army school, I joined a tank battalion in Germany where I carried out the normal duties one would expect from a young officer, i.e., platoon commander, and subsequently also a deputy company commander. I was then called to exercise the position of what we call S1, so personnel officer, and adjutant to the battalion commander. Following that I was called to return to military academy to be first the deputy and then the commander of the first years in the polytechnic division, the 146th polytechnic promotion. And after that in September 1992, I joined the Ministry of Defence, more specifically the military intelligence and security service where I carried out various duties, mainly military intelligence analyst.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could we call up Exhibit number -- Rule 65 ter number 2858.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. Let me address something you've just mentioned. You are a member of a service at the OTP with -- together with other analysts. How many analysts are there in that team, in that section?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the number has -- has decreased over the past years, but I think in average we're around 12 to 14 analysts who each support different cases. For some cases there are more analysts. I would like to add also in this context that the report I compiled is only my work, so nobody else in the team or outside of the team was involved in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who is the head of the analysts' team? Is there someone who is the head?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. The head of the team is Mr. Philip Coo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is the geographic representations? Are there Americans, Belgians, British? Can you tell us the distribution by country among these 14 analysts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think that the geographic distribution of the team reflects the -- kind of reflects the composition of the United Nations. There are indeed, I think, one or two Americans. There is a Ukrainian analyst, a Philippino analyst. There are I think two people from -- or three people from the United Kingdom. There is Dutch analyst, there's a Belgian analyst, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question. In terms of ranks, the head of your service, Mr. Philip Coo, what sort of rank did he have in his own country and what are the ranks of your colleagues? What ranks did they hold in their respective country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not familiar with the ranks of all my colleagues, but I know that Mr. Coo, I think, was a captain or a major in the Canadian Armed Forces, whereas Ukrainian colleague was a Colonel in his armed forces. For the other people I would -- I'm not so sure. I think there is at least one non-commissioned officer. I also forgot to add that there is a Hungarian colleague who was, I think, a Captain or a Major in his armed force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes. I'd like to call up if we could 65 ter number 2858. Your Honours, that's also in the binder you have. You'll see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, is this your --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I demand that the Prosecutor say each time in which binder the document is, because there are three binders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, Mr. Marcussen. Please give the number of the binder. This document apparently is in binder 3, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think there have been a miscommunication. We have -- in binder 3 we have the CV of the expert and his reports and related documents. And then we have -- in binders 1 and 2 we have the exhibits that we intend to use today. That might be a little counter-intuitive, and I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, is this your CV?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, this is my CV for court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: If we could go -- if Your Honours go to the second page. If we could go in e-court to the second page of the document. I can see under item 5 that you have also served for some time outside Belgium. Could you give us a brief explanation of what you were doing.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. From December 1994 until October 1995, I served in the headquarters of UNPROFOR, which later became known as UNPF in Zagreb. When I arrived there, my first task consisted of updating orders of battles, so the structure of the armed forces in the area, the information that was held in the office on that issue, but because the person in charge of that -- of the team I worked in, the military information team, understood that I had actually more experience than most of my colleagues, I was then tasked to work in a sub-team known as the assessment team where I carried out the activities that are listed in the CV. If you want, I can specify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes, please, if you --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Mr. President, we don't have it all in Serbian, and your administrative employees who are supposed to put it on the ELMO don't have it either. That document stops somewhere halfway down the page in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you've raised two points, and there's one thing I'd like to mention. On several occasions you say "your employees," "your associates." Please note, Mr. Seselj, that I don't have any employees. I don't have any associates. In this Tribunal we have three organs that are completely independent, one from the other. You have the Office of the Prosecutor, the Registry, and the Trial Chambers. The only associates I have are the Trial Chambers' assistants and legal officers. All the others are completely independent from me. I can't give any instructions or orders to the Registrar or to anyone else except during the proceedings. So when you use the word "employees," "associates," you might give the impression to those listening to us that the Judges here have -- completely command everything that happens in this Tribunal. You've said that on a number of occasions. I don't know if you have something in mind when you use that sort of language, but I wanted to make that very clear. The Judges only work with the senior legal officer and the legal officers of the Chamber. The Judges have no power over anyone else. And when it comes to giving grades to their own assistants, the Judges only give advice. They don't have the final say on that matter. I wanted that thing to be extremely clear. Second point: Yes, you're right. We don't have a B/C/S version of the witness's CV. If there's a problem in that respect, the best way to proceed is probably to put the CV on the ELMO, to ask the witness to read out the relevant passage, and then the interpreters will translate the relevant passage in Mr. Seselj's language.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: We seem, Your Honours, to have a technical problem with the CV that we have in B/C/S, but maybe Mr. Theunens could simply explain what his functions were. I'm not sure it's essential that -- that we -- we necessarily look at the CV for the explanation of his tasks. And I will ensure that we get a copy of the CV to the accused in his language very quickly. It's being printed, I'm informed, right now and the accused can be given a copy. Let's -- if we just wait for a second, I think it's being produced.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, since we have time to spare while the document is being delivered, I hope you will allow me to explain what I thought when I said "your employees." Maybe it's a problem with interpretation. When I say "employees," I mean all the administrative personnel cooperating with the Trial Chamber in conducting proceedings. Assistants, associates, employees or whatever it is called in your environment, but it is absolutely inconceivable to me that you may think that I have ulterior motives in saying that. I'm not trying to insult any of the administrative personnel here. When I say that they're your associates, I don't think that I'm insulting you either. I didn't mean they're your private associates. When I address you, I address the whole Trial Chamber and the Court as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens. Now that we have sorted out this issue, would you please continue with your explanation of your -- your duties while your serving with the UNTAES -- sorry, UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, my duties while serving with UNPROFOR can be summarised in three -- under three headings. First of all, we would follow, analyse, and assess the military developments and to a certain extent also political developments in the zone of operation of UNPROFOR and its subordinate forces, i.e., the peacekeeping force in Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and FYROM, former Yugoslavia Republic of Macedonia. We would then participate and provide oral or written briefings - I mean, that would be done by myself or colleagues - daily briefings to the operations section within the UNPROFOR command, also daily briefings to the force command and the senior, if I can express myself that way, civilian leadership of the mission. And then we would also prepare written documents both for internal use, I mean within the UNPF, UNPROFOR headquarters, as well as for external use. Sometimes there would be questions from the Security Council or from other UN organisation officers, I apologise, who would then go to the civilian component, i.e., the special representative of the Secretary-General or to the force commander who would then forward -- if it was a matter that was within our competence would then forward the question to us. And my tasks also included liaison within the headquarters between military and civilian agencies, mainly civil affairs and political affairs, and we would also, when possible, go out in the field to have meetings with our counterparts in the sectors, I mean as UNPROFOR is organised, or the battalions and to see for ourselves what the developments were. And to summarise, mainly whereas the people in the operations department would follow the developments, we would use that information to try to prepare predictions, i.e., an outlook how could the situation develop and what would be the implications for the overall situation in the area in general but also in relation to the peacekeeping forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And then from -- in 1996, 1997, you served with UNTAES in Vukovar, Croatia. What were your functions there?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. The United Nations Transitional Administration for Eastern Slavonia was a much smaller mission than UNPROFOR. Its zone of responsibility was limited to the area known as Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, and I basically carried out the same tasks as I did in the UNPROFOR UNPF headquarters with a slight change in focus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And then again in 1998, 1999, you served for a while in the region. Could you elaborate a little on that function.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. From December 1998 till April 1999, I served as the chief of the Belgian National Intelligence Cell in the SFOR, so the Stabilisation Force headquarters in Sarajevo, which was essentially a national assignment. So I was not part of that force. And my duties, in addition to managing the team or leading the team or the cell, as well as following and analysing the developments in the zone of interest, also consisted of intelligence liaison between various governmental and non-governmental agencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: If we could go back to page 1 of the CV, please. You -- I can see that from September 1997 to July 1998 you attended a staff course. What level was that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is the senior officer candidate course, and it's a course at -- for the ground force at brigade level. So basically you are trained to operate in a brigade staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And lastly about your CV, you have an Licentiaat. What level of degree is that translated into in English?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the framework of the Bologna Agreement which regularises university degrees within Europe, the degree of Licentiaat, or Licencie in French, from the military academy is equalised to a master's degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender Mr. Theunens' CV.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. I have a question with respect to your CV. I see that from April 1997 to June 1997 you attended for about three months a training programme in Washington, DC, and here we see Defence Intelligence Agency. What is that? What was this training all about? Can you give us some information about this, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. So the training consists of two components. The first component is a study of the US intelligence community, which covers a number of agencies, both civilian as well as military, so we learned about legislation that guided or directed the activities of these organisations and their interaction. The second component of the course is an analysis course on the strategic level, so where the students are trained in techniques of strategic analysis. I would like to add that the course -- or the students were people from all over the world. They were -- there was an Albanian officer. There were people from Thailand, from other countries in Asia, from Latin America, from Europe, and as well as US civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And who were the trainers? Was it the CIA? Was it another body? Were these people from other governmental agencies? Who were the people directing the training?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the course was organised by the defence intelligence agency which is, as the name says, is the main intelligence agency within the armed forces in the United States. The trainers or the teachers were people from various backgrounds. There were university professors. There were people from the various organisations which are part of US intelligence community. So there was for example a speaker of the CIA. There would also -- which I didn't mention we would also visit newspapers and political parties so we would have briefings from, at least, journalists from the two main newspapers in Washington, DC. We would visit the Republican party, the democratic party and get a briefing there. So it was very varied, if I can express myself that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Can we have a number, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number P191.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And now I'd like to call up 65 ter number 2854. And this should be in binder 3. It should be in the same binder as the CV, the second tab there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's the thin -- it's the thin of the three binders that you received, if there's any ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, the document you can see on the screen, is that your expert report?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Sorry, I think we have on the screen the addendum, which is 58 -- 2854B -- A, sorry, but what we should have is -- we should simply have 2854.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, now I think we've got the right document up. Is this -- is this the report that you have prepared?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, it is. It's the table of contents now on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, in preparing this report, what was your -- what were you asked to give an opinion on?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I received the following question from the senior attorney -- senior trial attorney, I apologise, who was at the time in charge of the trial, of the case, the question was to look at the role of SRS/SCP volunteers in the conflict in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, more specifically in relation to the areas that are included in the indictment. And also, secondly to study or to analyse the relationship between these volunteers and Mr. Vojislav Seselj or the organisations he was allegedly in control of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: In preparing your analysis, which structures did you look at?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, when I received that question which was quite general, I first started to collect information in order to improve my understanding of the question, and I realised very soon that one could not consider the topic in isolation, i.e., that these volunteers were part of a bigger thing, and therefore I thought it would be useful to include in the report also information on the SFRY armed forces. I also included information on the situation in Serbia in relation to armed forces. And I also realised very soon that it was important to make a distinction between the de jure aspects, i.e., the situation as it was described in the legislation and the doctrine, as well as between what I would call the de facto situation. And I mean by that the way how this legislation and doctrine was implemented during the conflict, focused, of course, on the activities of these volunteers and the other forces. They operated in cooperation, subordination, or other relations with -- during that conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did your analysis also -- did your report also include an analysis of -- could we call it the structure of the opposing forces in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. This report is solely focused on SRS/SCP volunteers, as well as, as I mentioned, the forces with whom they operated together in various relations which are explained in the report, and I can be there more specific. It's the SFRY armed forces consisting of JNA and TO, and then what I would call local Serb TO or police forces that were created in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, as well as the TO of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, you told us that you were asked to investigate into the role of the SRS in the conflict in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, more specifically the relation to the areas that are included in the indictment and also to analyse the relationship between these volunteers and Mr. Seselj. My question would be if you analysis also intends to analyse the relation between the SRS volunteers and the JNA.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. Just for the transcript, I was asked to investigate in the role of SRS volunteers, not SRS as a party, and obviously the relationship between the SRS volunteers and the JNA in the various areas is an essential component of my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question. It is a direct follow-up of the question asked by my fellow Judge, and this is my question: You testified in the Milosevic case. You know that Mr. Seselj also testified in the Milosevic case. I was not able to check whether you testified before him or after him. As far as you remember, could you tell us when you testified in the Milosevic case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I testified in -- if I'm not wrong, in January 2004, during the Prosecution phase of the Milosevic trial, whereas Mr. Seselj testified during Defence phase, which was later. So he testified after me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So he testified after you. Have you -- do you know of his testimony, and do you know of his opinion on the links between the SRS and the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. I am familiar with Mr. Seselj's testimony in the Milosevic case, and I'm also familiar with contemporaneous statements of Mr. Seselj on the relationship between SRS/SCP volunteers and the JNA, and I have attempted to include them in part 2 of the report, in section 3 which deals specifically with the SRS/SCP volunteers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you're telling me that in this report that we have there are some parts of the report that incorporated what was said during the Milosevic trial, said by Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. I may have misexpressed myself. The report only includes what I would call contemporaneous statements of Mr. Seselj, i.e., statements he made at the time of the events or shortly after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So I'll come back to my question then. Your report as we have it here never took into account what Mr. Milosevic or Mr. Seselj might have said regarding these volunteers, the role played by the JNA, and the role played by the other paramilitary units or the role of the TOs of a number of municipalities. This was not incorporated into this report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, maybe I have to clarify something about the methodology applied. The footnotes that are included in the report only reflect a fraction of the material I reviewed. The footnotes reflect the material I considered relevant for the subject matter I was requested to analyse. While preparing the report, and I'm not sure any more whether Mr. Seselj testified in the Seselj trial before the report was filed or afterwards, but he certainly testified before the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj testified in the Milosevic case, not the Seselj case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I apologise. In the Milosevic trial. I'm sorry. What I meant to say is that he certainly testified in the Milosevic trial prior to the filing of the addendum, which means I was familiar with his testimony in the Milosevic trial. I was also familiar with, for example, Mr. Milosevic's cross-examination of my -- during my testimony in the Milosevic trial, and that is -- and maybe we'll come back later to that when we explain the methodology that was applied. That --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So in the addendum you took into account a number of data that had emerged during the Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will try to explain it better. The fact that there is no explicit reference to the testimony or -- in the addendum or in any other part of the report does not mean that I didn't take it into account. It is information like any other information I consulted while preparing the report, and the report then is a reflection of that process --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'm asking all these questions through evidence that had already been admitted by this Chamber, which is the entire testimony of Mr. Seselj in the Milosevic case, and there was 15 hearings involved, more than 60 hours of testimony. I sum up in two -- and this is what seems to transpire from the question and answers that we have in this testimony: First, at the time, Mr. Milosevic did not have any military authority over the JNA. This is at least the version that seems to emerge from their Q and As. Secondly, the generals of the JNA were in control of all military action. That's the first thing. Second thing which seems to emerge from this document, the Serbian volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party were under the authority of the military command either of the JNA or -- or for those -- for others, Republika Srpska. That's all we have coming out of this testimony. So were these two elements integrated into your own report or maybe in the addendum? This is what I would like to know. Or did you just stick to your report which had been written before the testimony of Mr. Seselj in the Milosevic case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was familiar with Mr. Milosevic's view on his relation with the JNA, as well as what the generals -- the powers that the generals allegedly had according to Mr. Milosevic, at the latest in January 2004 when he cross-examined me in the Milosevic case. Now, the documents I have consulted, as well as other sources, but the report itself is only based on documents, do not support these views in relation to Mr. Milosevic. For Mr. Seselj's views are concerned on the relation between SRS volunteers and the JNA during the conflict, he made certain statements already at the time of the events, that his volunteers after September 1991 were always subordinated to the JNA and that the JNA "was our army." These statements are included, or the main ones are included in part 2 of the report, section 2, and in the English version that starts on page 24. So where I provide an overview of quotations from statements by Mr. Seselj. In the report I have also included military documents, orders from military commanders in the various areas, situation reports, which show that indeed most often SRS/SCP volunteers, while participating in the conflict in Croatia are subordinated to the JNA. Vukovar is a very good example. However, there are also documents from senior JNA officers, as well as later for Bosnia-Herzegovina from VRS, so armed forces of the entity known as the Republika Srpska, and these documents include orders and reports where these VRS officers state that they have no control over SRS/SCP volunteers. So in summary I would like to say -- or in conclusion I would like to say that indeed the statements are included with the comment that the statements Mr. Seselj made during the Milosevic trial were actually nothing new when compared to earlier statements and that the documents from -- military documents from people on the ground do not always support these statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for your answer. I think that you have given us the scene and the backdrop, and we'll be able to understand the rest of the proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question. If I understood you well, you've also analysed the relationship between Seselj's volunteers and the army of Republika Srpska. I would like to know whether you also analysed the relationship between Seselj's volunteers and the broader institution, which was the -- the Serbian armed forces. Was there a higher command that was -- if I understood you well, there was a superior command at the Serbian army level. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure whether I understand your question well, but I will try to summarise which forces were acting where and what relationship were. The events --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. In your report I understood that there was an entity, the Serbian armed forces. This entity was made up of the JNA and of the TO. So in this whole construction or device I have not really understood, and I'm sure we'll understand it later on during the examination, but I would like you to know that I have this problem that I would like solved. I don't really understand the role that it plays in this whole contraption. You have the JNA and the TO. On top you have the armed forces, and I don't understand how the volunteers fit in to this whole structure. Not just Seselj's volunteers but all volunteers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to maybe make my -- the question a bit more specific, but you seem to be having a difficult time. My fellow Judge, if I'm not mistaken, is talking about the Serbian armed forces, the question of the Serbian armed forces, which is a very broad concept. Within this entity there would be JNA, on the one hand, and the TO. But in this concept of the armed -- Serbian armed forces, where do the volunteers fit in? That's the whole question. This is our question. This is the essence of the question: These volunteers, are they 100 per cent integrated into the JNA or into the TOs or -- and then if that's the case, they are part and parcel of the Serbian armed forces; or were these volunteers another entity, a de facto entity or de jure, maybe, we'll see. It all depends on the documents. We'll see according to the documents. So it would be in addition to the JNA and the TO, like in a parallel structure. Above, under, where does it fit? That's the whole question that we have.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. I understand the question. I would just like to make a small correction. When we talk about the JNA and the TO, according to the 1974 constitution and the 1982 All People's Defence law, these were the two components of the SFRY Armed forces, so the armed forces of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The constitution and All People's Defence Law also stipulate that under certain circumstances the armed forces, JNA or TO, can be replenished with volunteers. Now, these volunteers are then people without military obligations who, for whatever reason, want to participate in the defence effort. When I say "certain conditions," I meant by that the three states defined in the legislation: The state of war, the state of imminent threat of war, or a state of emergency. Now, the law also says, the All People's Defence Law, that the TO will include of armed formations which are not part of the JNA. It is also stated that anyone who takes part in the defence of the country in case of an aggression will be considered a member of the armed forces. Now, what is important in the context of the report is that in the course of 1991, political parties in Serbia, the same way it happened in Croatia or Bosnia-Herzegovina, but that's not the subject matter of the report, but certain political parties in Serbia start to recruit, organise, dispatch, participate in the training of volunteers, and these volunteers are then sent in groups to the area of conflict. Two important aspects, it is that -- those are that we talk about volunteer groups who are being sent. Some of these groups, as is shown in part 2 of the report, try to act as separate formations, whereas other groups become subordinated to the JNA. But I think that the distinction between individual volunteers and groups is very important in the context of the report. A second important aspect is that we see these volunteers appear in the conflict areas before the legal conditions as they were defined in the '74 constitution and the 1982 All People's Defence Law have been fulfilled. It is only on the 3rd of October, 1991, that the SFRY Presidency, and I will try to quote the text as it is in the document: "...establishes the existence of a state of imminent threat of war." But even before that condition was fulfilled, we saw that there were volunteers on the ground. Another important aspect which should clarify the role of political parties is that based on the documents I reviewed, many of these volunteers who were recruited by political parties were actually conscripts. So they should have, if the law had been applied, they should have joined the armed forces, because -- i.e., the JNA or the TO, because there had been mobilisations, call-up and so on; but as I tried to explain in the second part of the report, for various reasons these people, i.e., these conscripts said, "Well, look, I don't want to serve in the JNA. I want to serve in the volunteer group or of party X, Y, or Z." In this report I take then a closer look at the volunteers that were recruited, dispatched, by the SRS/SCP through the organisations it controlled. I hope that that clarifies the matter for you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It clarifies this. I'm trying to sum it up maybe so that it can be on the transcript. You just said that according to the law enforced, there are three states that could solve this problem of the volunteers, of the conscripts: State of emergency, state of imminent war, or state of war. And you're saying that according to what you studied, the text which was applied was only applied on October 3rd, 1991. That was when there was imminent threat of war. That's when there was the proclamation, and that's the founding text. And you're saying before October 3rd, 1991, volunteers were already on the field. And so in your mind, and I'm sure we'll come back to this, you're making a difference between individual volunteers, so individuals who volunteer on their own accord to go and join either the JNA or the TO, and other volunteers that are grouped. And these groups of volunteers, they join the JNA or the TO but through their political party. Is this it? Is this what you said? Did I sum it up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, that is correct. And if you allow me just to be complete --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not an expert, but I'm trying to understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, just to be complete, I would like to add that between August 1991 and December 1991, the government of the Republic of Serbia, the Federal Secretariat for People's Defence, as well as the SFRY Presidency, adopt decrees or decisions in order to what I qualified in my report as regularise the situation on the ground. And we see, for example, that on the 18th of August, 1991, the government of the Republic of Serbia adopts a decree for the registration of volunteers in the TO, so the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Serbia. In September 1991, the -- the General Staff of the SFRY armed forces issues an instruction for the acceptance of volunteers into the JNA. And on the 10th of December, 1991, the SFRY Presidency adopts the presidential order number 10 for the engagement of volunteers during the state of imminent threat of war. Based on my review of the documents, only the last reference I mentioned, so the 10th of December SFRY Presidency order, makes a reference to volunteer formations. So this is the first time that we see the term "formations" or "group" being used in a legal document in the context of volunteers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. One last question and then I will give the floor to the Prosecutor. This term "volunteers," it's a bit surprising for those who are used to, you know, Western armies and the way they operate, the UK, Belgium, France, Denmark, Sweden, the US, and so on. This concept of volunteer does not exist in other -- in all these countries I mentioned. Did you look into this to see whether maybe it's not a concept that would come from the Communist state, you know, in Communism? So I have in mind, you know, Mao Zedong's books on People's war, the fact when there's a conflict everybody must join, become a soldier. So why didn't your report look into this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. You see the terminology, the use of terms like volunteer more in the concept of, for example, guerrilla warfare as you mentioned with Mao Zedong or with Che Guevara and I consulted the works of these two individuals in relation to guerrilla warfare, but actually the laws that existed in Yugoslavia were, in my view in conclusion, sufficient to deal with the issue because the report starts in part 1 with reference to the concept of All People's Defence, or which is ONO in Serbian, which is sometimes translated -- so All People's Defence, ONO, which is sometimes translated as total national defence. And this concept as is explained in the report was published first in 1969, and basically it means that the whole population participates in the defence effort. Okay. JNA are the federal armed forces. Then in the republics a Territorial Defence would be established, but, in addition, there would also be Civil Defence which is dealing essentially with civilian matters; for example, these are activities after natural or other disasters or war damage. There is also, when you consult the All People's Defence Law, a monitoring and warning system. So I considered guerrilla warfare, as such, was less relevant in the conflict -- excuse me, in the context of the report than the concept of All People's Defence or total national defence. Whereas, and I can give you the reference, in Article 119 of the 1982 All People's Defence Law, which is 65 ter number 19, the concept of volunteers is legally defined. And I apologise for being so extensive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this explanation which makes things much clearer. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Maybe now that we are at your conclusions, just to cover one last point that we would also come back to, but what is your conclusion on the -- on the reporting structure or the contacts between these volunteer units of the SRS and SCP that were sent on the ground and the accused and the leadership of this organisation?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, in part 2 of the report there is a section on the SRS War Staff, and I deal with the various aspects of the relations between the SRS War Staff and the SRS/SCP volunteers starting with recruitment and training, and this actually starts on page 32 in the English version, and it goes to page 58, if I'm not wrong. So I start with training. Then I talk about the role in dispatching or the sending of these volunteers, i.e., the deployment. I talk about equipment, military equipment including weapons. I also talk about payment. And then there is paragraph, a title -- or subtitle "Relationships," starting on page 47, where I give examples -- at least one example of what I described as the exchange of operational information from volunteers on the ground to the SRS War Staff. There is on page 51, for example, 65 ter number 486 where I quote from a report Srecko Radovanovic, who is described as the deputy commander for the defence of the villages of Sodolovci, Koprivna, and Petrova Slatina, so this is page 51, part 2 in the English version, and he sends a report on -- containing detailed operational information on the situation in the zone of operations where he and his volunteers are active. There are also other examples, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, what you're saying is very interesting. You're saying that the volunteers would send reports to the SRS War Staff. That's all very well. And you've mentioned two occasions when a report was prepared and sent. While I was listening to you, I was making the connection with what's currently happening in Iraq. You have US soldiers sending text messages or calling their friends or family in the United States to tell them what they are doing. In today's world with today's communications, that type of information can readily be sent and received, but these reports you mentioned, did they -- were they made after a specific order, an order that had been issued for these reports to be prepared? And in other words, was there a double chain of command? Let me give an example. Let's assume that a US soldier in Iraq sends some information to a friend who is a member of the Republican or Democratic Party. It does not mean that that party has sent him an order to do so. So that's my point. You mention these reports in your own report, but did this report come after an order, a document, that had given specific -- specific instructions to these volunteers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, in relation to the Iraq situation, I would like to clarify that if a member of armed forces sends operational information to people outside the chain of command on matters they are dealing with operations, that would actually be a violation of security, because operational matters are in general classified, and they are sent through classified reports via secure communication means through the -- to the authority that has a need to know. On page 50, part 2, English version of the report, I have a subtitle 4: "Fact-finding Missions by members of the SRS 'War Staff' to the conflict zone." This is followed on page 51 by a discussion of 65 ter number 459 where, and I'm reading from the report: "Zoran Rankic," whose function is described as "Deputy Staff Commander," states in his report that he was -- he went "... by the order of the Staff and the President, Vojislav Seselj, with the task of visiting the units in the field and relaying an order to withdraw in order to regroup the forces." And this report is dated the 2nd of September, 1991. So here we have a clear reference to an order by the War Staff and more specifically by Mr. Seselj. The earlier document I refer to, 65 ter number 486, we would have to look at the entire document to see what the basis was for Radovanovic's report. I didn't quote the entire Radovanovic report in my report. I only included the sections that I considered relevant in this context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Mr. President, I think the expert witness should show these documents, because he has at his disposal all the documents he's quoting from. I think it's very important when he mentions a document that he also show it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I believe we'll come back to the issue of these documents later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. That was actually just what I was about to say. Both of the reports that are mentioned are in the binders that you have, and it was my intention to cover these. And as I can see the break is approaching, I have prepared for Your Honours and for the accused an outline of my examination of this witness, and maybe that would be helpful to indicate the areas that I will be covering, and it would also have references to the relevant exhibit numbers. And of course we have a translation into B/C/S of the accused, but I'm not providing one to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will review the document during the break. Mr. Seselj will read the document as well. It's almost time to take the break, so we'll have a 20-minute break, and we'll resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The hearing is resumed. Just a technical information for next week. We will start at 9.00 and not at 8.30. So we'll start at -- we start at 8.30 when we have to sit also in the afternoon, but next week we will not have any sittings in the afternoon, so we can start at 9.00 next week. Very well. Now I give the floor to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I hope it will not be too much of an anticlimax, but I'd like to go back to discuss the preparation of the report a bit more in detail. Mr. Theunens, we have talked about the scope of your analysis. What I'd like to move on to now is the sources that you consulted. You've already touched upon some of the types of documents you -- you looked at, but could you give us a brief overview of the material that you have consulted in preparing the report.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the materials I consulted in preparation of the report broadly covered the following categories: I looked at SFRY legislation; SFRY armed forces doctrinal regulations as well as manuals; then military documents by JNA, TO, VRS consisting of reports and orders. I also included documents and reports by organs of Ministry of Interior. For example, for what the entity known as Republika Srpska is concerned. I also consulted open sources, i.e., documents which are available to the public, more specifically the party magazine of the Serbian Radical Party, Velika Srbija. Sometimes other media other reports. And just to -- to finalise, I only included documentary evidence in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you also have access to documents originating from the SRS/SCP?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes indeed, Your Honours. I forgot to mention that. The section on the SRS War Staff is largely based on documents that were issued or directed to the SRS War Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could you describe the process by which these sources -- no. Excuse me. Maybe I should, just before I move into the list, clarify. The material that's included in the report, is that all the material that you looked at for your analysis? You have answered this maybe already, but just for clarity.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. As I mentioned earlier this morning, I looked at a much wider range of information including also testimony, witness statements, and other material which is available in the Office of the Prosecutor. I also consulted the internet for certain searches. But the document itself only -- is only based on documentary evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Were any limits put on your access to the evidence in the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: No, there were not, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now could you please describe the process by which these sources were transformed into your report.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the methodology I applied while compiling the report is the same one I applied when working as an intelligence analyst and is commonly known as the intelligence cycle. The intelligence cycle consists of four phases. The first phase is direction; secondly, collection; thirdly, processing; and fourthly, dissemination. In the context of this report, the processing phase, the processing phase, yes, indeed, is the most important one, and it covers four steps which -- or five steps, excuse me, which I can explain if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Maybe if you could just give us a brief description of these stages so we understand how you -- what methodology you applied in your analysis.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: You mean for the intelligence cycle or for the processing --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: For your processing of the documents you have selected for your report.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Okay. The processing phase starts with collation of the information. So the direction I received from the general tasking, i.e., a report on the role of the SRS/SCP volunteers and so on, as we explained before. Then I started to collect information. During the collation step, actually in the processing phase, you organise the information in a way and you record it in a way that it's easily accessible. Secondly, in the processing phase the evaluation is carried out. Evaluation covers the assessment of the reliability of the source and the credibility of the information. Next, after the evaluation, we're going to analyse the information. We're going to -- during the analysis step, we are going to review the information in order to identify significant facts. Once we have done that, we're going to interpret these facts. What do these facts mean? In particular, in comparison to the earlier knowledge we have. And then lastly, in the integration step of the processing phase we integrate. We include the new information within the existing information, and we amend or we review our conclusions or assessments if necessary. Now, just to finalise, the intelligence cycle is mainly applied for predictive work. I mean, an intelligence analyst is generally requested to explain future developments, whereas I had to explain events that have already happened, but that, in my view, does not affect the methodology that is applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Is there any difference in the nature of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. I have listened to you, because what you're saying is quite interesting regarding intelligence analysis. You did use a method, you know, to analyse something that already happened, whereas usually this is used for -- for the future. If I've understood well, there are five phases, but I missed one. You've got assessment, analysis, interpretation, and integration. Where's the fifth phase?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the fifth phase is actually the first one is collation. It's more -- it means that you record the information and you organise it. It can consist of the establishment of databases. It can also consist of just putting the documents in binders by topic. It's just to facilitate the further use of that information. So it's not really a thought process. It's more like a logistical kind of aspect. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. You said that you had -- first there's direction, collection, processing, and dissemination. That's what you said; right? Those are the four steps. And then you said that in processing there are five steps, and I'm missing one -- these are the steps I'm interested in. In processing there are five steps. What are they exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So in processing, Your Honours, the five steps are collation, evaluation, analysis, integration, and interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This technique is used worldwide in all intelligence departments, or is it a Belgian technique? Does it come from the US?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wouldn't be able to -- to answer the question in relation to all services in the world, but it's -- at least it is applied in the services I'm familiar with. And in addition, I have also noticed that, for example, when you search on the internet you use intelligence cycle. I find the web site of Notre Dame university in the United States which actually had the processing phase -- excuse me, the processing, yeah, phase explained and also in relation to the evaluation of sources for its students, and it was even a teaching course in university in order to assist students in assessing the reliability of sources and accredibility with the information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for this additional information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, after you finished your report have you had an opportunity to review the report?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. The report was finished in March 2006, so at a later stage an addendum was prepared, and also more recently we discovered that there were some typographical or other minor errors in the report and a corrigendum was therefore prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, dealing first with the addendum. First, for the record, the addendum is -- we don't need to call it up on the screen, but it's 65 ter number 2854A, and it's included in the binder after the main report. And, Mr. Theunens, why did you prepare the addendum?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I prepared the addendum because after the finalisation of the report in March 2006, additional documents became available which I considered relevant in the context report, and therefore they were included in the addendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And to -- did the documents that have become available, did they change any of your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: No, they didn't, Your Honours. They were in line with -- or they confirmed or supported the conclusions drawn in the initial report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And then you mentioned that you had discovered some minor typographical errors and an addendum was filed -- sorry, a corrigendum was filed. The 65 ter number for the corrigendum is 2854B. Mr. Theunens, last night did you become aware that there were some minor mistakes in that version?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Sorry. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: For Your Honours we have -- in e-court we have replaced the addendum, and I'd like to hand you -- what shall we call it? A corrected version of the correction. And I have also a copy for the accused.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Mr. President, I think you should take certain steps towards the Prosecution because this expert report was ready in March 2006, as the witness tells us. He even wrote an addendum to this report, then several days ago he submitted corrections, then last night he established there were still some mistakes remaining. That means that the report is actually not ready. It's not complete. You should return it to him to submit it in a complete form. Maybe there will be more corrections today, tomorrow. Who can guarantee there will not be many more corrections to follow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there are a few corrections that I have just seen. They are minor corrections, and maybe the Prosecutor can review them very quickly. We all have the document. Page 10, paragraph 31, and so forth and so on. I mean this does not deal with the substance of the report anyway. For example, he wants to change quorum to vote, responsibility with authority. So, Mr. Prosecutor, could you please quickly review these corrections with the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: If I may just clarify one thing. The document that has just been handed out is a corrected version of the corrigendum. There are no new changes per se being made. It's simply that the main error was that there's a reference in the first version to page 76 of the report. It should have been 67. It's really minor little details that the expert discovered, and frankly in the context of a document that's 400 pages long I would submit that these are inevitable things that happen and only speaks to the thoroughness with which the expert has worked in preparing this, and there is no prejudice to the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness, when you reviewed this report, obviously you noted that there were a few typing errors and there were words that you wanted to substitute with others, but the substance of the report is untouched.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, at the end of the testimony of Mr. Theunens, I will ask that the report with the addendum and the correction be admitted into evidence. I will also be asking that all the documents, all the exhibits that are referred to in the report be admitted as underlying documents. This is just for your information. I'll deal with that at the end of the testimony of the witness. So what you have received in the binders and the exhibits that -- I will be tendering along the way as we move through the witness evidence is part of what we would seek admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, would you please explain to us which are the key laws that regulate the armed forces in -- that regulated the armed forces and [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the key legislation regulating or defining the SFRY armed forces are the 1974 constitution as well as the 1982 All People's Defence Law and its amendments that were issued later. So this law defined the armed forces. They regulate the use of the armed forces as well as command and control in the armed forces. In -- in addition there's also the 1985 Law on the Service in the Armed Forces which regulates the service in the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, we have included the constitution of former Yugoslavia or excerpts of it in your binder and also the All People's Defence Law. They are 65 ter numbers 10 and 65 ter number 19. If we could call up 65 ter number 10 first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen, at Exhibit 10 we only have a few articles of the constitution. We don't have the full constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. Your Honour, we have attempted to include only the most relevant parts of some of the bigger documents that we're seeking to tender. In e-court we have the full -- we have the full version of the documents as exhibits. It's simply for logistical reasons that we have not wanted to burden you with too many binders. Excuse me. And, Your Honours, I was not intending to go into the substance of this particular document. I called this document up just so that it can be seen that this is from the Official Gazettes of the former Yugoslavia. And without going into the actual document I was going to request that this document be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a number for the constitution, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That will be Exhibit number P192.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And I'd like to do the same with the All People's Defence Law. So that would be 65 ter number 19. Maybe if Your Honours just want to consult the B/C/S version to see that it's from the gazettes and then I'd like to tender it into evidence without calling it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens -- I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a number for Exhibit 19.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit number P193.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, what was the mission of the armed forces of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: The mission of the armed forces -- of the SFRY armed forces as defined in the constitution and the All People's Defence Law was to defend or to protect the territorial integrity, the sovereignty, the independence, and the social order in the SFRY armed forces, and this is explained in Article 92 of the 1982 All People's Defence Law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Theunens, I'd like to move on to the topic of command and control. Did the armed forces of the former Yugoslavia apply this concept?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, and there are two components in -- in this topic. First of all, command and control over the armed forces, as well as command and control within the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And if -- we will get into that in a little bit, but maybe first could you explain what the core principles of command and control in the Yugoslav Army was? It's explained in part 1 of your report at pages 28 through 90 -- sorry, 28 through 31, and in the B/C/S version it's pages 29 through 32. I'm not -- don't call this up, but could you just explain what the principles were.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: First, the Article 112 of the 1982 All People's Defence Law defines the three principles which are single command; secondly, unity in command; and thirdly, the obligation to implement decisions, commands, and orders of a superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Is -- are these principles similar to what is applied in, for example, in the Belgian army?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. I -- without exaggerating I think I can say that these principles are universal in relation to the application or implementation of command and control by armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And why do armed forces have these principles? What's the purpose?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Because they are considered essential in order to implement the mission the armed forces have been given by, in general, the political authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, I would like to call up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are dealing with the issue of command and control, and I'm thinking here of the Serbian Radical Party. Please have a look at Article 94 of the law. I'd like everyone to turn to Article 94 of that law. And mention here is made of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia that is entrusted with special, specific responsibility. And when we look at this article, Witness, we see that a political organisation played a role in the operation of the army. Article 94.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: In the English version I can see -- in e-court the English version it should be page 62, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not working with the e-court system. I'm working on the basis of hard-copy documents. I find it too risky to work with the e-court system, but now it's displayed. So we can all see this page on screen, and we can see that this political party that at the time was the only political party, we can see that type of responsibility was entrusted to the League of Communists. Witness, was your attention drawn to the role played by the League of Communists, and when the League of Communists stopped existing and was replaced by other political parties weren't these parties, according to Article 94, weren't these new parties supposed to exercise some form of command and control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, when looking at that article obviously I viewed at the entire All People's Defence Law in the framework of the preparation of my report, but this specific article in my view is part of -- has to be seen in context of the overall situation in the SFRY as it was not only in 1982 but as it was still in 1991, and actually until April 1992 when the SFRY ceases to exist and is formally replaced FRY, Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and where the JNA is replaced by the VJ, the Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sir, but what I was driving at is that in the mind-set that prevailed in the former Yugoslavia, the political party, and here it was -- there was just one political party, but a political party would play a role in the armed forces in -- when the former Yugoslavia was dismantled, the League of Communists did not play a part any more, but what I would like to know is whether other political parties like the Serbian Radical Party, whether these parties did not wish to continue, to continue operating in the same way as had been the case before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, my reply will include several aspects. The importance of -- of Communist doctrine was already clear from the structure from the SFRY armed forces. That means that on -- from battalion level upwards you would have within the command officers for morale and political guidance who would obviously promote the values that were considered important in the framework of the political situation SFRY within the units. I think it's also important to highlight the importance of the slogan of "Brotherhood and unity" which dominated the whole situation in the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and was also very important within the armed forces. Now, the situation you are referring to is the situation that starts to exist from, let's say, the end of the '80s or early '90s onwards, and it is a transition phase. There are still political and moral guidance officers in the commands and that's also something, I think, that is visible through, for example, the book of army General Kadijevic which is quoted in the report, how on one hand senior JNA officers still believe in Yugoslavia and in Communism, whereas, on the other hand, there are political parties, nationalistic political parties, who start to criticise the JNA because they say JNA is -- is Communist and so on and so on, and we want to have our own army. We don't want to have Communism any more, and they try to infiltrate the armed forces, or actually as could be linked to the establishment of volunteer groups, try to create -- some call them party armies or at least volunteer groups that are mainly motivated by a nationalistic or an ethnic ideology instead of the JNA, which was driven or -- by a Communist ideology but also by the slogan of "Brotherhood and unity," which is also visible from the various legal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You looked into the operation of the JNA at length. Can you tell me if like in other socialist or Communist armies there were political commissioners in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I mentioned, Your Honours, within -- at least -- or starting at the battalion level upwards, within the command of the unit whereby the command consists of the commander and his assistants from brigade level onwards we would have a staff and assistant commanders, well, there would be an assistant for morale and political guidance. And even in Western armies we would have morale officers but they would not be part of the command but they would look at troop morale. The officers for morale and political guidance has a clear role. You could compare him to the political commissioners as you call them, but they are there to ensure that -- yeah, Communist doctrine or call it socialist doctrine is being implemented. And it's actually also visible through the principle of one of the three principles of command and control, the principle of unified command and control. Throughout the chain of command from the highest level to the lowest level, to put it in simple terms, everybody works in the same direction, and this direction is determined to a large extent by the -- by the political doctrine or the political ideology that exists in the country at that stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've stated that in the brigades there would be someone in charge of morale and political guidance. I'd like you to tell me the following: Before all the problems started, before the country was dismantled, in the JNA was there a link between this officer, this particular officer, and the League of Communists outside of the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the documents I have reviewed while preparing this report have not indicated that such a link, a formal link, existed. I can imagine that there would be seminars or courses or similar things whereby morale officers would be regularly updated on political ideology, but I have not come --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course you understand why I'm asking this question, because if there was such a link before, then we might think that with the SRS volunteers integrated within the JNA that there would be a similar link between them and their political party based on the way things were organised before and that link between the League of Communists and the relevant officers within the JNA.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe to clarify, Your Honours, there may have been a formal link in the sense of exchange of information or -- between the -- the political guidance and morale officer on one hand and the League of Communists on the other hand, but I have seen no indication whatsoever that this link would interfere with the chain of command. However, the links that may have existed between certain JNA officers or officers in the TO and the Serbian Radical Party, if they existed and where they existed, those would be de facto links which were obviously not foreseen by the doctrine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have one question. These officers who were in charge of morale, they were not taking part in military operations, did they, in the field?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
