utterances.text: It is correct that they would not command -- normally not command -- or de jure not command forces in the field, but they would -- they would certainly participate in the planning process of operations as any other member of the command, because their -- their input and their views would be -- could be relevant for the commander when he receives a task from his superior which he has to implement, and their input could be useful like the input of any other member of the command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question to follow up on this question put by my fellow Judge. These officers in charge of morale and political guidance, you said they would take part in planning and maybe debriefing of operations. They took part in meetings at the command. I'd like to know the following about them: Before 1982, 1985, do you know how they were appointed to their position? Were they appointed to their position by the League of Communists or by the military authority? You may not be able to answer that question because it's a very technical question indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honours, I cannot answer the question because I have not looked into that specific matter. But just to summarise, when preparing the report and coming across documents prepared by these -- such officers, I have never seen an indication that these officers would interfere or would participate in the chain of command except for providing guidance to the command or assisting him or had another operational role.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Maybe the next exhibit will be on point. I'd like to call up 65 number 24. And go to e-court page number 104 in the English and e-court page 60 in the B/C/S. It is in your binders. It would be the second page of -- of the document that you have on the list under tab 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, do you have a copy of the exhibit in front of you?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: It's coming up in e-court, but as we all have it on paper, could you explain what this is? Well, first of all, maybe where it comes from. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the chart is an excerpt from a manual that was used within military academies in the SFRY armed forces called the "Command and Control." It dates from 1983. And the chart shows a -- what I would call generic command structure above the level of battalion. When you take a closer look at the chart you see the commander and his command consisting on the left-hand side of the staff whereby the staff is directed or managed by the chief of staff. You have a number of staff sections. And then we move -- when we move to the right we see a number of organs, three of them, which were also known as assistant commanders. We have the organ for political guidance with an assistant commander, the security organ, as well as logistics organs. So the heads of these three organs would be assistant commanders where the chief of staff he would be the only deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And what role would these different organs play in the planning process in the army?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Well, all of these organs participate not only in the planning of -- of operations but in the daily or the continuous work of the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's something that strikes me when I look at this organisational chart. The military court, military prosecutor, investigating judge, military investigating judge, they're all under this -- they all come under this organ for political guidance, in charge also of morale, and they don't come under the security organ or the chief of staff. Why is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the dotted line actually means that there exists a relationship or there are contacts but it doesn't imply a subordination. I have some information on the military courts and the military prosecutor in part 1 of the report when I refer to the 1977 laws on these two organs. It is correct that security organs, one of their tasks would be to investigate serious crimes against the armed forces. During the conflict security organs were also involved in the investigation of serious crimes including violations of the laws and customs of war, and they would, together with the military police, enjoy particular relations with the military prosecutor and the military court. When reviewing these documents on these reports on crimes, I did not come across information on -- on any role for the morale or political guidance organs in the investigation of these -- of these crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But why is it on a dotted line then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because, Your Honours, because it shows a relationship which is not a command relationship. It can be an exchange of information. It can be consultation. Bodies can exchange information or can have contact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're saying it's not command, but the title is "General structure of command."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours, but "Command" is here used as a noun. It's not the verb "to command." It's the name of a structure, the command. So the staff and the organs are identified, and then also with the dotted line in this particular situation there is a link to bodies which are relevant in the context of describing the command. But, for example, there is no link between the commander and the military court. So the dotted line means contact, exchange of information or another form of contact, but not subordination in this context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, just to clarify something, I'm sure it's obvious but you said the role of the security organs was to investigate crimes against the armed forces. Is it also the role to investigate crimes by the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, that is correct. And in part 1 of the report I -- the section number -- the section on laws of armed conflict, I discussed that aspect. Page 55. Sorry, page 55 in the English version, to be complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, was my understanding correct of what you said before that these different units within the command, so artillery, security, and these different units would provide input to the commander in the preparation of plans of, for example, a combat operation?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours. In -- command and control is not static kind of thing. It's a process whereby the commander has to continuously gather information. At the same time, obviously, the information is observed. Decisions are made on a continuous basis and orders are issued. The commander himself cannot do all these tasks and he needs assistants for that and though assistants are described in this chart. For example, when the commander receives from his superior a particular order to carry out an attack which involves the use of -- or an important role for artillery, well, the commander will direct himself via the chief of staff to his expert for artillery in order to assist with the planning of the use of artillery for that specific operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'd like now to go to Exhibit 65 ter number 540. 540. Oh, sorry, could I ask for an exhibit number, maybe, for 65 ter number 24 before I move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit number P194.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, you have a copy of this -- and now it's also on the screen. This is an example of an order. What I'd like you to explain, comment on, is how we can see -- if we can see the work of these different sub-organs of the command appearing in this document, and for that I would -- first of all, there's data on the enemy here. Where would that come from?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the data on the enemy can come from -- from several sources. It will come first and foremost from the own forces in -- that are fighting in that area. I say first and foremost because I'm influenced by this specific -- specific context of this order. It has to do with Vukovar. But it will come from the own forces who are fighting the -- in a particular area and who have information on the situation there, in particular on the enemy. Now it will come from -- it can come from the higher echelons. So this is a brigade level order. Guards Motorised Brigade was subordinate to the 1st Military District, so the 1st Military District has intelligence on the situation. They included in their order to the subordinate commands. This information will be reviewed by the intelligence officer who is a member of the staff. He may have other sources. He may have established a network of his own sources. The information can also come from neighbouring units and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And if we flip over to page 4, which I think in e-court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we move to page 4 there's one detail from page 3 on description of the enemy, on the fourth paragraph. I see that it is said that women and children were trained with the sniper guns. Have you seen that? Sniper rifles. On page 3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. It's the third page in English, page 3. So this is -- intelligence is -- can be based on facts that have been observed and which have been reported by different sources. It can also include an assessment. Here it appears to be something that has been observed and that has been considered relevant to include in the order. Now, we cannot determine which source provided this information, what the reliability was of the source or the credibility of this information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But isn't there a risk that there could be misinformation, false information, or information planted, false information planted in this kind of report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This risk exists, Your Honour, but within the military there were -- excuse me, disciplinary measures could be taken in case of misinforming the superiors, and that refers in first instance to the commander when he sends incorrect reports to his superiors. Now, as I said, the first data on the enemy is intelligence. Intelligence can be wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if I may, let me go into military technical details. When a unit learns suddenly that the enemy may use a sniper, snipers to shoot at them, but then these snipers could very well be women and children. Does this have any consequences, military consequences, regarding civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I mean from the purely military point of view it would mean that -- the message would mean that one has to be extra careful when seeing women and children. Now, if these women and children are armed and participate in the conflict, they could be considered combatants.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Then on page 4, which is on page 2 of the B/C/S, we have what I believe is the order "I have decided." And then on the next page -- the next pages there are different tasks given to the units. And then when we come to page 7, and if we see from 7, we have intelligence; 8, we have security -- sorry, on page 8 we have security and engineering, on page 9 we have logistic support, on page 10 we have a section on command and communications. So this is -- is this the practical implementation of the input from these different organs that you talked about before in the command?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. This is the end result of the planning process, and it's -- yeah, this is then the written order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And then at the end there's a section on reports at various different points in time. Now -- and the order is, in this case, signed and stamped. Is -- is this kind of a document -- is that a standard order, standard military order of the kind that you have been looking at?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. Orders are prepared in militaries I'm familiar with in accordance with a template, and it is in the interests of everyone to always use this standardised template because it facilitates not only the drafting but also the implementation of the order. The fact that reports have to be submitted is directly linked to the fact that in accordance to not only SFRY armed forces doctrine but also doctrine of other armed forces, the commander has to be aware of the situation in his zone of responsibility. Sometimes it's called situation awareness. And one of the source -- or -- for this situational awareness are the reports sent by the subordinates and more specifically reports on the implementation of the order which is part of one of the functions of command and control, the inspection function.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And now that we are on this exhibit, you have referred to this document in your report in what context?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I used this -- this order in my report in the second part on the report when discussing the operations in Slavonia, Baranja, Western Srem and more specifically in Vukovar because it is an order by the Guards Motorised Brigade for an attack, an order for blockade, an attack, in Vukovar dated the 1st of October. I also used this order because it mentions the Petrova Gora TO detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And so this order is also an example of -- it illustrates the command and control relationship between the JNA and the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. On -- in paragraph 5, unit tasks, we see the acronym JOD, Jurisni Odred, which is Assault Detachment. In part 1 of the report I explain what Assault Detachments, Operational Groups, Tactical Groups are, but basically these are ad hoc formations which are established to carry out a specific task in a specific context at a specific time. And one of the advantages of these ad hoc units is that they facilitate command and control, because when you look at 5.1, Jurisni Odred should be number one. It mentions units of the Guards Brigade, the 1st Motorised Battalion. It also mentions at the end with guidance from Petrova Gora Odred TO. So with guys from the Petrova Gora TO detachment. It also mentions Military Police Battalion, elements which have all been subordinated to these various forces I mentioned under the command of the 1st Assault Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender this exhibit as well. So that is Exhibit ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P195.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One technical question. We're talking about the Petrova Gora TO. In this order does it state very clearly that in this offensive operation the TO is fully subordinated to the army? Is that what this document tells us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. And with "army" we mean the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another technical question. I found it striking that the order is drawn up by a lieutenant colonel. Is it customary for an officer of such a high rank to draft an order himself unless we are talking about a large-scale operation and the order was drafted at very high level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. JNA orders -- the JNA orders I have come across, at the bottom of the order on the right side the commander signs because he is responsible. The commander rarely drafts an order himself. So this as it concerns a brigade operation, it's in principle the chief of the operations department of the brigade staff or a member of that department who will draft the order and then it will be typed by somebody else. And we don't see the B/C/S on the monitor but normally the B/C/S will have just the initials without mentioning who drafted it or who typed it, but the initials are sufficient to see who drafted it and who typed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But here in B/C/S, in the B/C/S version, we have Lieutenant Colonel Lukic mentioned and we have the name of the person who typed the document. It's also an officer. Very well. Yes, you're right. Usually we find initials in these documents and here we have the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now I'd like to move now from the principles and the implementation to the structures through which they were implemented. Mr. Theunens, what was the highest body of command and control in the armed forces of former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: The SFRY Presidency and more specifically the president of the Presidency was the Supreme Commander of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if you want to follow on paper, in page 20 -- page 20 of the English version of the expert report, and that would be on page 21 in the B/C/S version, you have an illustration of this. In e-court it is Exhibit 2854, e-court page 43 in English and e-court page 41 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, could you explain what this diagram should illustrate?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this diagram illustrates the command structure during one of the three states, state of emergency, state of imminent threat of war, or state of war, whereby the SFRY Presidency with its eight members would constitute the Supreme Command presided by the president of the Presidency, and the Supreme Command would be assisted by a Supreme Command Staff which consisted of the federal secretary for People's Defence, the Federal Secretariat for People's Defence, as well as the General Staff of the SFRY armed forces which was led by the Chief of the General Staff of the SFRY armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Who were the members of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Well, each -- each of the six constituent republics had a representative, as well as the autonomous provinces, the two autonomous provinces or regions, and the president of the Presidency would be elected among these eight members for one year.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Were -- so the Presidency did not -- was not composed of the presidents of the different republics. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: That is correct. For example, yeah -- sorry, you want me to give the names or --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: If you could also do that. First I just want to confirm whether they were the presidents of the republics. You've answered that.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: No. The members of the Presidency had been appointed or elected by the republics. They obviously maintained relations with their republics, but they were not the presidents of their republic. For example, Borisav Jovic, who I quoted from, was during the first half of 1991 the president of the Presidency. He was at the same time the representative of Serbia, but he -- he was not the President of Serbia because Slobodan Milosevic was the president of Serbia. In Croatia the situation was similar, as in any republic, but there I can give the names. Stipe Mesic was representative of Croatia in the SFRY Presidency, but Franjo Tudjman was the president of Croatia at that time. And the same applies to the other republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And so for Serbia, for example?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: As I said. So Borisav Jovic was the representative of the Republic of Serbia, but Slobodan Milosevic was the president of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we are starting to deal with the very significant issues, and we should dwell on them a little longer. We have the constitution from 1974, and reading this constitution we understand that the Presidency is the supreme command and control organ or body. That's what we can read in the documents we have before us. At the time in 1991, you gave us the name of the president of the Presidency. It was Jovic. And you said -- as an example that the Croatian representative within the Presidency was Mesic. You added that at the time the President of Serbia was Milosevic. Now I'm looking at the text here of the document, and in terms of command and control, Mr. Milosevic was not the first in line. It was the Presidency that was in charge of command and control. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, but now we enter in the area of de jure versus de facto situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm -- myself, I'm in the de jure area. De facto is something else. I'm looking at the texts, and if you look at the texts you see that command and control is the Presidency, is in the hands of the Presidency. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And actually, that article you quote from is Article 313, which refers clearly to the situation that existed when Tito was still alive. Article 328 of the 1974 constitution clarifies that it is the president of the SFRY Presidency who, on behalf of the SFRY Presidency, is in charge of command over the armed forces of the SFRY. And that is what the law says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Talking about the command and control de facto, if there is de facto command and control structure, isn't -- can't we talk about a constitutional coup? Because if according to the constitution command and control has to be in the hands of the Presidency but actually others are in charge of command and control, then we are faced with a problem. What do you think? You are the expert after all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, section 1 of part 2 of the report clearly tries to depict and describe the problem that exists, because we can see that there are serious problems with the functioning of the SFRY Presidency. The sources I consulted for this section are mainly -- are two books. One book by Borisav Jovic, so the Serbian representative in the Presidency and the outgoing chairman, as well as the book of Veljko Kadijevic, who was at that time the federal secretary for all people -- for People's Defence. And indeed when reading these books, and I've tried to include the most significant aspects in my report, one can see that there is indeed a problem with the functioning and the authority of the de jure Supreme Command body, i.e., the SFRY Presidency and, more specifically, the president of that Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe it will assist actually the next exhibit is the book by Kadijevic. It is 65 ter number 1758. And if Your Honours would turn to page 20 of that exhibit, it is one, two, three -- it's five pages into the excerpt that we have included in your binder. And for the accused, it's just a few pages in, two or three.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: In the first paragraph -- well, Mr. Theunens, I think -- do you have this in front of you? Yes, you have.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I have it indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Have you quoted -- have you particularly looked at this part book in your report?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And what does that -- what is this showing about the question we're just talking about now, the situation in the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: It shows that specifically for Kadijevic, that he as the chief of the staff of the Supreme Command does not recognise Stipe Mesic as his Supreme Commander. Now, I think it's useful to also consider other sources, for example, the book by Jovic and to see how Jovic describes these events to get a completer picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And we will move to that in a little bit because that's the next exhibit, but in the e-court -- well, the events that are being described here by Kadijevic, when did they take place?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: When did the -- about what time is this crisis happening?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: This crisis is happening concretely mid-May. On the 15th of May, Mesic should have been -- or -- yeah, elected as chairman of the SFRY Presidency, but he failed to be elected by his -- by most of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would seek to tender Exhibit 1758 at this stage.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number P196.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: To be sure, Mr. Theunens, which year were we talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 15th of May, 1991. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen, you're asking for Exhibit 1758 to be tendered into evidence. Are you asking for -- for just the pages we have here to be tendered, i.e., page 2, 3, 20, 38, 39, 40, 41, and so on and so forth, or are you asking for the entire book to be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: This particular book is, I think, so significant that I would suggest that the Chamber may want to have the whole book. Otherwise, I would -- I can also propose to do excerpts, but I think there are a few pages that we need then to add just for context, but it's not a lot, like four or five pages, if Your Honours prefer that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Mr. President, I propose that the entire book be admitted into evidence because I will make extensive use of it both in the cross-examination of this witness and in some other situation -- situations. As the OTP has had the entire book translated and has tendered it, I move that it be admitted in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Has the book been fully translated into English or into French? Has the book been translated into one of the working languages of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'm afraid it has only been translated into English, the whole book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're asking for the book to be tendered into evidence, and Mr. Seselj also wants the entire book to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I think in light of what has been said by Mr. Seselj -- I'm happy to go just with the excerpts, but I'm in your -- in your ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber has decided that the entire book will be admitted into evidence. We'll ask then the Prosecution to provide the additional pages. Can we have a number, Mr. Registrar, for the entire book?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit number P196.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: How many pages are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About 150.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm just checking because I don't know by heart, but by the ERN you are -- almost 150.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it's page -- 150-page book, roughly. Is that -- is that the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes. That's the translation. Yes, about that size.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, you also referred to the diary of Mr. Jovic as relevant context for this particular topic. That diary, we have excerpts in -- we have excerpts in the binder you have under the next tab. The 65 ter number is 2093. Mr. Theunens, could you explain what it is that the diary show about this particular issue, the crisis in the Presidency? What -- what happened when there was this rejection of Mr. Mesic?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is the published diary of Borisav Jovic, so the president of the Republic of Serbia and the outgoing chairman of the Presidency, and he gives his view on the crisis and he states, for example, that Mesic could not be elected. What is also interesting particularly in the context of your earlier questions, Your Honour, when you read the book and analyse its contents it shows that parallel meetings are ongoing. And I reviewed in particular the situation during -- between May 1991 and end of 1991, and I came to a total count of approximately 27 meetings whereby Jovic, Milosevic meet with Kadijevic and/or with Blagoje Adzic. Blagoje Adzic is the Chief of the General Staff of the SFRY armed forces, and he was during the second half of 1991 also often the acting federal secretary for People's Defence because Kadijevic was regularly absent for health reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, did you prepare an overview of -- or a table indicating the meetings, the 27 meetings that you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, that table I will hand you a copy of, and a copy to the accused, of course. And that -- the witness should, in all fairness, also have a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, could you explain what it is we see in this table? In the first row there are a number of dates, and the crosses indicate what?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: The dates come from Jovic's diary, and the crosses refer to meetings where the people for whom a cross is mentioned in the column, or is included in the column, are present at this meeting. For example, on the 9th of May there is, according to Jovic, or according to what Jovic writes in his book a meeting between Jovic, Kadijevic, and Milosevic. On the 10th of July there is a meeting between Jovic and Kadijevic. On the 5th of September, for example, further down, there's a meeting between Jovic, Kadijevic, Adzic, and Milosevic. These meetings are interesting or relevant in the context of this report for the -- for the subject matter that is being discussed, and as I've tried to summarise in my report, during some of these meetings instructions are given by Jovic and Milosevic to Kadijevic on the use of the armed forces. For example, on the 5th of July, 1991, and this is discussed on page 6 -- English page 6 in the second part of my report. I forgot to mention the 27th of June, as well as other dates that can be found back in my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, nothing escapes me. You said on page 67, line 6 and 7, that Kadijevic was not there for health reasons, was absent for health reasons. And in the chart that we now have, in this table we now have I see that Kadijevic is supposed to attend all meetings from May 9 to December 25, 1991. And I see that Adzic attends on May 15th, June 24, and then as of August also, but with interruptions on September 24, October 2nd, October 22nd. So the chart is wrong. The table is wrong. It's false. If Mr. Kadijevic is ill, he can't attend. So why is there a cross as if he was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, when you look at the dates there are -- obviously there are gaps. So the people mentioned in the table are not meeting on a daily basis. Now, I don't have an exact record of Kadijevic's absences, but all I can say is that according to the entries in Jovic's book, the crosses show that these people met at that day. I can imagine, for example, but it's maybe too speculative, that Kadijevic is absent, say, on the 3rd and the 4th of October, but he can well meet on the 2nd and on the 5th. And that Adzic is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But the consequence of this is that Kadijevic attended all meetings, all 27 meetings.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, there may have been many more meetings. These are meetings which Jovic mentions in his book. They are not necessarily official Presidency meetings. Most likely they are not official Presidency meetings because otherwise Milosevic would not attend. So these can be informal gatherings. These can be meetings that one of the four people mentioned in the table has called. But the only relevance of the table is to show that on date X, according to Jovic these people met and discussed certain issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, you -- in your book you specifically discuss the meeting on the 5th of July, 1991. Could you please explain to the Court the significance of this meeting for your analysis?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. The meeting for the 5th of July which is mentioned in Jovic's book, during that meeting Jovic and Milosevic, so the Serbian representative in the Presidency and outgoing chairman, as well as the president of the Republic of Serbia, they make a request to Kadijevic, federal secretary for People's Defence and chief of staff of the staff of the Supreme Command, on the deployment and operational role of the JNA. And more specifically, they request to concentrate the main forces of the JNA along a line, which we may see on a map. Anyway, in the west Karlovac to Plitvice, in the east Baranja to Vinkovci, and the Sava in the south and Neretva, in order to concentrate the JNA along the areas or along a line that delineates the areas that are considered Serb by Jovic and Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, you explained earlier the legal framework for command and control in the armed forces. Is instructions from Milosevic consistent with that framework?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: No, it is not, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Is it -- sorry, I just lost my place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think as the break is coming up we should -- before we go to the break, I would like to tender the excerpts of Exhibit 2093, so that is Jovic's diary, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the chart. And the chart, and that table too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And the table has been uploaded into e-court. It already has 65 ter number 7174.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Mr. President. I consider that Borisav Jovic's book as relevant evidence cannot be admitted along with this expert report. The Prosecution must call Borisav Jovic himself as a Prosecution witness and tender his book through his testimony. Jovic's book was created after his conflict with Slobodan Milosevic and caused his expulsion from all offices in the Socialist Party. So it can be a matter of mutual political showdown. Jovic would have to be brought to testify to this rather than have this witness explain the contents of the book as if it were taken for granted that everything in the book was true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Chamber has deliberated and dismisses this objection and is admitting not the entire book by Jovic but only the excerpts that were commented by the witness. Mr. Registrar, we need two numbers, one for the table with the 27 meetings and another one for the excerpts that we find under number 2093 in the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The -- the table with the 27 meetings will be Exhibit number P197, and the excerpts of the diary will be Exhibit number P198.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will now break. We will resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The hearing's resumed. We will continue until 1.15 p.m., but at 1.05, I will ask the witness to leave the courtroom because I think the Prosecutor needs ten minutes in private session. So we'll stop the examination-in-chief at 1.05 p.m., and it will resume next week. I give the floor to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may for a minute very briefly to put forward a procedural issue. In the break I received a submission by the Registry based on Rule 33(B) concerning the translation of books, on the 7th of February, 2008. The Registry is informing me that they have not yet submitted the books for translation. They are asking you to confirm the order for the books to be translated and I see they have found agencies who will do this for twice or three times the amount of money required by the agency I have found. And here you can see that the Registry is doing this and yet you are telling me, you have told me many times, that I am not having documents translated and so on and so forth. Until the Registry translates these two books which are the basis of my defence case, I have no reason to submit any other documents for translation. That's all I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Registrar has seized us, according to Rule 33(B) of a request to confirm it is one of our decision made and ordering for 10.000 pages to be translated, because they came up with quotes starting on this decision, and we have a high quote and a low quote, and the Registrar is asking us to confirm whether we really want these 10.000 pages translated and what is the price range that the Trial Chamber is looking for. We will very soon rule on this. You yourself, of course, can write your own submissions -- just to reconfirm orally what you want. And next week we will rule on this. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a small correction. You gave me a total quota of 10.000 pages of translation. These two books have only 2.000 pages. Ten thousand pages is the overall quota, all the documents put together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. That is true. The Registrar's document only deals with 2.000 pages, not 10.000. That's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Chamber is going to look into this once again, and the Trial Chamber will have to answer the requests coming from Registry, and we will answer, but now let's continue with the examination-in-chief, and I give the floor to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I gave you a handout. I think we have covered a number of the things in that handout, so I'm going to jump down a little bit in the overview, if you're following where we're going on that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, you -- you described that you have -- sorry. You have already described that the armed forces of the former Yugoslavia had two components, the JNA and the TO. What was the command relationship, if any, between the two?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, according to doctrine if units of the JNA and the TO would operate in the same area with the same mission, there would only be one command in application of the principle of single command and control. This would mean in practical terms that in most scenarios or in most, yeah, scenarios for operations a JNA officer would be in command. However, there is at least one situation which was described as the temporary occupation of the territory, i.e., that the enemy has taken part of Yugoslav territory, and then a TO officer could be in command. This makes sense from the military point of view because TO units were mainly local units, i.e., manned by people from the area, and they would know the area, which in this case would be occupied by the enemy best.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Would you just -- could you explain briefly what the units coming under the Supreme Command were? If we move from the Supreme Command, what would be the main units -- or entities moving downwards in the JNA structure? At the time relevant to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes. It would be helpful to have the chart, but I can do it without a chart. So when you move from the Supreme Command and the Supreme Command Staff, the Supreme Command Staff orders the military districts. There were three army districts as well as a military -- a military naval district, as well as the air force and the air defence. And the Military Districts would then be composed of corps, divisions, brigades, and then you go downwards, brigades, regiments, battalions, companies, and platoons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And if you could just clarify the geographical structure of the Territorial Defence. What were the main components of that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Territorial Defence was organised by republics, so each republic, as well as autonomous region or province had its own Territorial Defence whereby the structure reflected the territorial structure. So from top to bottom you would go from on the staff level from Republican staff, zonal staff, regional staff, Municipal Staff, and these staffs would then be in charge of the units, various levels going from lowest level platoons to the highest level brigades. And also a distinction would have to be made between local TO units, which was the majority of the TO, as well as mobile TO units which were, according to one source, only 20 per cent of the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: In the last group of military formations, you have already touched on the ad hoc groups that you describe in your report. You mentioned them this morning, but would you please just sum up. Which ad hoc groups are you familiar with in the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: This is discussed on page 41 in the English version of the report where I provide an overview on the JNA doctrine in relation to Operational Groups, Tactical Groups, and Assault Detachments. As I explained this morning, in particular operational circumstances it was considered useful to change the arrangements in order to facilitate the execution of the task as well as the implementation of command and control, in particular in areas where, for example, it was -- where the terrain was difficult or where it was difficult to communicate with each other, and therefore these kind of ad hoc groupings would be set up which actually also exist in Western armies where we have the concept, for example, of battle groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: At -- at pages 45 to 61 in the English version of your report you describe in quite some detail the application of various disciplinary laws and implementation of international humanitarian law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. I see that you're moving on to a different topic, and I have not understood anything about these ad hoc groups. I was wondering if you had thought of the possibility of ad hoc groups being made up only of volunteers. Well, Witness, could you tell us what these ad hoc groups were? Can you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will try to be, Your Honours, and maybe I can explain it with a practical example. The Vukovar situation is a very particular situation because it is -- it is an operation conducted in an urban environment, urban warfare, so warfare in a city. We see when we look at the situation there between end of September 1991 and the fall of Vukovar on the 18th of November, 1991, that on the side of the JNA, if I can express myself that way, we have different kinds of units. We have the Guards Motorised Brigade, which is normally subordinated to the Federal Secretariat -- secretary, excuse me, for Peoples Defence but there you're subordinated to the First Military District. We have units of the 1st military districts and units of the TO of the Republic of Serbia but we also have units of what I would call the local Serb TO, i.e., you can call it remnants or self-established formations which may well have been part of the TO of the Republic of Croatia prior to the conflict but now have become separate entities who do not respond any more to the authorities of the Republic of Croatia, but they want to fight alongside the JNA. And we have also volunteers and both volunteer groups as well as volunteers included JNA units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: If I may interrupt you for one minute, I'm sorry. If Your Honours would like to look at Exhibit 622 which you have in your binder and we can maybe call it up in e-court as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So, Your Honours, you see an order here from Operational Group South, which, and is explained in my report, is based on the Guards Motorised Brigade. So the Guards Motorised Brigade has the command of OG South but it also includes other units, other brigades which come from different establishment units. So we have an ad hoc arrangement where we have units coming from different establishment or parent units who are supposed to work together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Can I stop you just for one minute just so we go through -- first of all where on this document do we see that this is an Operational Group?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Because on -- on the left top heading it says "Command OG," Operativna Grupa, and then it says "Jug." "Jug" stands for "south."

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And when you say we see different groups involved, what part? You're referring to item number 2, for example?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes. I was not yet at that level. I was mainly giving the background information but we can go to item 2, to units' tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes. And so could you explain what these different units are, how that --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah. So the Operational Group consists of different units which are not necessarily all establishment units or units which are normally part of the Guards Motorised Brigade. In addition, the Guards Motorised Brigade has resubordinated. Instead of being subordinated to the federal secretary for People's Defence they are now under the command of the 1st Military District. In order to -- because of the size of the group, the Operational Group is much bigger than the brigade, we are operating -- that's the first factor. Secondly, we're operating in a particular environment. We are operating in a city which in general makes it difficult to exercise command and control, because on one hand you're acting in a very small area but, on the other hand, it's much harder to see each other. It's not the same as launching an armoured attack in -- somewhere in the plains. These factors require the establishment of -- of particular -- the implementation of particular command arrangements where you create an ad hoc groupation, Operational Group with its subcomponents, which are under a particular command. Okay. In this specific case the command of the OG consisted of the command of the Guards Motorised Brigade. I've seen other Operational Groups where the command of the OG is an ad hoc arrangement including officers from, for example, the commands of the subordinate units who may well for the first time work together in this particular context. So it helps to have a special command established for those circumstances, in particular when you're operating in a particular -- or in a specific environment like a city. When you go into paragraph 2, "units' tasks" we see Assault Detachments. Assault Detachments are also ad hoc arrangements. Now, according to JNA doctrine an assault detachment can be established, for example, when you want to attack a fortified facility and you want to include JNA elements and TO elements. An assault detachment would have the size or could have the size of a battalion. Could also --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: No. And in this particular assault detachment we're looking at now, what units do we see? We have a -- could you just go through them and -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: We see that the assault detachment consists of the 1st Motorised Battalion. Then we have the 1st and the 3rd Company of the 2nd Military Police Battalion. We have the Leva Supoderica police detachment which and will become clear later is a TO detachment with particular links with the SRS War Staff. There's also the TO detachment Petrova Gora, as well as a unit known as the volunteers company Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And where is Novi Sad?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Novi Sad is a city in Serbia. The first city you see close to Danube, important city. There's also armors included as well as other elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, and here we have been talking about just the issue of Operational Groups and what it means.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: This particular document you mentioned in the context of Vukovar, and it identifies in your view the units that were involved in the attack in -- yeah, operational in the area of Vukovar at the time that's relevant to your report?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes. And to be more specific at the time of that order. When the commander says "units' tasks," well, all the units he mentions there are subordinate to him, so are his units, and he's responsible for their activities while they are subordinated to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Including the volunteer units?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Exactly. Indeed, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please, before that. I have two questions to the witness. Mention is made here of the Assault Detachment made up of various units, motorised battalion, Military Police Battalion, and also Leva Supoderica. It's a unit headed by Kameni. But I see that mention is also made of Petrova Gora. Who are these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, Petrova Gora is another -- what I describe as local Serb TO formation in Vukovar. Petrova Gora refers to a geographic area, and so people from that area considered it important or useful to establish their own TO unit or detachment and which is then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We see that we have volunteers coming from Novi Sad. Were these volunteers of the SRS or are we talking about different volunteers here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this -- in the specific context of Vukovar and also taking into account the documents I reviewed, these would be other volunteers. Now, while doing research for this report, obviously I tried to find more information on -- on this unit, but I haven't been able to find any information their allegiance. The only thing we know is it consists of volunteers coming from Novi Sad and who decided they wanted to participate in the fighting in Vukovar and they are subordinated to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that mention is made of one tank, M-84. Who did this tank belong to, to Novi Sad or to the Motorised Battalion? Where did that tank come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, that tank would come from the armoured battalion of the Guards Motorised Brigade. The Guards Motorised Brigade had two motorised battalions -- excuse me, three motorised battalions, two military police battalions which made a very special unit, as well as one armoured battalion, and obviously supporting elements, engineering, artillery, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can see as well that another detachment is mentioned, another Assault Detachment, and I see here the following: "Ustasha forces." What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't have the exact -- I see it here. Well Ustasha is the name that is used to identify the opposing force and this would be then taken into context members of the Croatian national guard as well as other members of the Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. They are identified that way there. Very well. Mr. Marcussen, you wanted a number. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit number P199.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, you -- in your report at pages 45 to 61, you have looked at the armed forces of the Republic of Serbia. In your report you describe a change to the constitution of Serbia which provided that the president of Serbia commanded the armed forces in peacetime and war. And similarly you mentioned the Serbian Law on Defence which provides that the president commands the armed forces in peacetime and in war. Now, based on your research, have -- were such armed forces established in 1991, 1992 -- sorry, 1990, 1991?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, just for the accuracy of the record, it is page 62 to 70 in the English version of the report. And to answer the question, no, based on my research I -- such armed forces were not established, and so the Territorial Defence was considered the armed force of the Republic of Serbia during that time period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: According to these laws, who were allowed to organise and reinforce, arm, equip, and train armed forces?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, Article 118 of the 1991 Law on Defence of the Republic of Serbia states that such tasks could only be accomplished by competent state bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, although no Serb or Serbian army was formed, have you during your research come across anything that leads you to believe that armed formations did exist in Serbia at this time?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honours. From the documents I reviewed, one can indeed conclude that there were armed formations existing in Serbia which participated in the conflict in Croatia and which were not foreseen or which were actually not permitted by the Law on Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And have you formed an opinion about who organised these formations?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed. In the context of this report, there is information included on the role of political -- certain political parties in the establishment of such formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Were these formations based on the material you have reviewed, were they supported by the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Well, overall -- as an overall comment one could say that they were at least allowed to exist. There are indications that some groups were the subject of investigation or even that they were prevented from continuing to exist, and I refer, I think, to the Serbian Volunteer Guard in specific references. Now, I focus my research on the Serbian -- on the groups that were affiliated with the Serbian Radical Party, and there the conclusion would be that there was cooperation with the Ministry of Defence and/or the Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Serbia in order to organise, equip, arm, and dispatch these units, as well as cooperation with the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the two laws that have been referred to, namely the constitution of Serbia and the proclamation on the Law on Defence are found as Exhibit numbers 2019 and 385, and I would like to tender these two exhibits. They're in your binder. These are -- again they're simply texts from the Official Gazettes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Mr. President, we see here a reduced, abbreviated version of the constitution of the Republic of Serbia. It is correct that the constitution of the Republic of Serbia stipulates the role of the president of the republic in the command of armed forces, but there is provision that says that as long as Yugoslavia exists, it is transposed onto the federal state. So during the existence of Yugoslavia, the Republic of Serbia, in fact its president, has nothing to do with the command of the armed forces. You should instruct the Prosecution to deliver to you the constitution of the Republic of Serbia and the translation, because I know the Prosecution has it translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have two problems. I would like to find these documents. We cannot find them. 2019. Can you tell us where it is exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: It should be the next document in your binder after the order that we just looked for relating to Vukovar. So the next -- the next one is 2019. Essentially Your Honours would have noticed that we tried to put the exhibits in the binders in the order that they are coming up during the examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But then this document 2019 on the constitution of Serbia, Mr. Seselj raised an objection regarding this, saying that there is an article that is not included in the text we have, and it provides for the following: If -- if Serbia has no army, then it's the federal army that takes over. At least that's what I understood. But we don't have the relevant article in the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the -- the version of the exhibit which is in e-court is the complete version this law. As I said earlier, what we have done for the purpose of this binder is to just include the excerpts that are most relevant to the Prosecution. I think we should include the full law. I'm sure that the accused will be referencing it, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Registrar, we need a number for number 2019, but that's for the constitution that is in full in the e-court system. Can we have a number for this?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit number P200.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And the second document was 385, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that 65 ter number 385 will be Exhibit number P201.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, one more objection. The examination-in-chief has to be consistent. The witness has already told you that Serbia did not have formed armed forces. You were offered an abbreviated document, a diminished document. I made an objection saying that the document is not comprehensive, and it prejudices its probative value. Now, it would be appropriate for the Prosecutor to show you the final clause in the constitution which contains that provision, that restriction. It would be important both for my objection and for the view you are ultimately going to take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you can come back to this during your cross-examination. During cross-examination, you will have opportunities to ask this question to the witness. "You said this, the Prosecutor did not say this. I'm showing you article X of the constitution and this and so forth." That's the way you should play the game. Please continue, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, moving to the topic of volunteers, now again you touched upon this this morning, but just to clarify and remind us, who would -- who were the members of the armed forces of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the SFRY armed forces consisted of the JNA and the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm talking about who would be the staff or the -- who would be soldiers, officers. Who would be composed -- who would be the individuals in the army?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prosecutor, I'm sorry to interfere and intervene, but we have to -- this is very complex. We have to keep things in mind. When you're asking a question and you're talking about armed forces of the SFRY or armed forces of the Republic of Serbia, these are very different entities, and we have to be very specific in order to avoid mix-ups. I heard very carefully what the witness was saying at one point in time and he told us in the Republic of Serbia there was no army or only TOs, TO units that volunteers would join. Three Judges here on this Bench are highly qualified. They have attended, taken part in a good number of trials, so this is not unknown to them. So be extremely specific, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. I have not -- yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Let me -- let me put the question differently. How would the army of the SFRY fill the ranks in normal circumstances?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, in normal circumstances there would be different levels of units. There would be units of level A, B, C, and these three categories refer to the level of professionalisation of these units, i.e., A would have the most professional personnel, whereas B and C the least. For example, the Guards Motorised Brigade was for the largest part professional with professional officers and COs, and then of course there would be conscripts, people doing their military service. There could -- there would be regular call-ups of units, in particular for reserve units where there would only be a skeleton structure in peacetime consisting of a few officers and other members of the command where then reservists would be called up, reservists being people who have accomplished military service and who are still subject to military obligations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Maybe to finalise, in addition, as we discussed, this Article 119 of 1982 All People's Defence Law states that people without military obligations can still -- could still join the armed forces in one of the three states, and these would be volunteers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but as a backdrop, you just told us, you just explained there were three types of units, A, B, and C, the highly professionals being the As. But the backdrop for the JNA during Tito's time, was JNA a member of the Warsaw Pact? Was it? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the date, but I think in -- sometimes in the '50s, Yugoslavia left the Warsaw Pact, and Yugoslavia or the SFRY became one of the most well-known non-aligned nation and also leading country in the non-aligned nation movement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Is it true or false, then, that the army of former Yugoslavia at the time was very numerous in terms of soldiers? Some could even say that it was almost at the same level as the armies in the Warsaw Pact or in NATO. What do you think of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. There were estimates at the time, and certainly still in the '70s, that the JNA was the third army of -- of Europe, for example. Now, I don't recall exactly what this estimate was based on, mainly manpower, so quantity or was it also quality, education, weaponry and so on and so on, but indeed it was considered a very serious armed force. And of course we cannot neglect the factor of the TO, which was size-wise much bigger, during conflict was to be much bigger in size than the JNA and which would carry out a specific part of the duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now regarding professionalisation, officers in -- were the officers in the JNA as able in terms of standards as officers in the UK or in the Russian army, in the Soviet army, or in the US, or was their level lower?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can only speak to the -- the officers I met while working here at the ICTY, as well as reviewing expert reports by other military experts -- by outside military experts, I wanted to say, and the impression I had from -- mainly from these reports but also my own [indiscernible], that the JNA officers were very well-educated. There were different levels of training, military academy and subsequent staff courses, so very well-educated and very familiar with military doctrine. And actually, of course the defence concept was different. You had All People's Defence, whereas in the countries I'm familiar with, we don't have such a concept. But otherwise, tactical and operational doctrine was very similar, and also the level of education, just based on what I have seen here in these reports, were all experts when they assess and analyse that level of education and training, as well as from own meetings with former JNA officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, one last question since you've -- in order to be an officer in the JNA, did you have -- did you have to be -- a senior officer in the JNA, did you have to be a member of the League of Communists or could you have a military career within the JNA without belonging to the League of Communists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I haven't looked at this issue in detail, Your Honours, but based on my recollection one had to be a member of the -- of the League of Communists to achieve the highest level of ranks. But I'm -- it's not part of the research of my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: In the time frame that's relevant to your report, were there staffing difficulties for the army of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. In particular, Veljko Kadijevic highlights that -- this aspect in his book where he talks about the problems caused by the poor response to mobilisation and call-ups, as well as also what he describes as the, I think, negative control of political parties who want to send their own armed groups to the conflict zone instead of having these members, the members of these groups, become part of the JNA or the TO as they should have been in accordance with the doctrine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, based on your reports -- sorry, based on your analysis were nonetheless volunteer formations incorporated into the JNA?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honours. I mean, before they can become incorporated they first have to exist, and I start with, I think, that aspect on page 74 of part 1 of the report, and it continues to page 76. I give names of units which -- or formations which became like commonly known in the latter half of 1991. There were groups who identified themselves as White Eagles. There were groups who were known as Dusan Silni and other volunteer formations as well as SRS/SCP volunteer detachments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And what was the attitude of the authorities towards these formations? You've stated that Kadijevic was not particularly keen on them at least in the beginning, but could you explain what your analysis has shown on this?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This is discussed on the second part of page 76 where one notices that on the level of the government of Serbia, based on an interview Miodrag -- Vice-Admiral Miodrag Jokic, who was then Minister of Defence in the Republic of Serbia gave. He was -- and this interview was actually discussed on page 78, this dates from 25th of July, 1991. Jokic is asked, "Well, what is your view about the creation of -- or the call, excuse me, the call of the Serbian National Renewal Movement, SPO, for the establishment of a Serbian guard"? And Jokic refers to the existing legislation to say, "Well, look, there is no need for party armies or for volunteer formations which are outside the armed forces. People who want to join the armed forces can do that in the existing units, JNA or TO." However, it seems that later on in the course of time, and this happens very soon, there is change in his attitude. And then one can see that actually these volunteer formations are not only tacitly allowed to exist but are even -- the members are even recognised, and it is stated that volunteers, well, will be considered members of the armed forces like any other soldier or other member of the armed force. Which -- I will try to shorten it. Which on one hand is in line with the law, All People's Defence Law, but on the other hand taking into account these are actually people who should be mobilised into existing JNA units, mobilised on an individual basis, but for -- but prefer to serve in -- in new formations which are not foreseen in the armed force which actually is a kind of peculiar application of the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: From a military perspective, is there -- is there a difference between having -- having volunteers incorporated individually into different units and having a volunteer formation as such deployed?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, and I will -- my reply will consist of two components. The first one we have already addressed, that is, what is the motivation of these volunteers? Based on the documentation I have reviewed and in particular for what volunteers that were included in SRS/SCP volunteer detachments is concerned, these people are mainly motivated by ethnic motives. I.e., they go to the conflict to, as they call it, defend Serbs, but in practice, well, they -- for example, they call the Croats Ustashas, they're there to fight Ustashas whereas the JNA stood for something else. The JNA stood for brotherhood and unity and when you look at the legal references tries to make a distinction of the individual nationalities and nations in Yugoslavia but says that it is the army of all nationalities. From the purely -- the second aspect of my answer, from the purely military point of view, it is much harder for a commander to exercise command and control over a particular group that is suddenly included in his unit than over individuals that are admitted on an individual basis in that unit. All -- this has to do with cohesion and as they say in French esprit de corps. Group cohesion and, as we would call in the military, Esprit de corps, is one of the essential factors for the functioning of a unit. It starts on the lowest level, the squad, then the platoon and so on. And when I refer to my own education and background, it was one of the first thing we had to do is to teach our soldiers, who could be professional soldiers but as well as conscripts, that they were part of a particular unit and that this unit was part of the a bigger armed force. Now, it is easier to do that with -- when individuals arrive and are incorporated into an existing unit than when you get a group with a very specific motivation which is not necessarily the motivation of the JNA, but you still need to include these people in your unit and you need to make sure that they do the things you want them to do in accordance with the motivation that exists within your armed force. Just to close this, there is a quite famous book about -- explaining the military failure of the United States in -- in Vietnam. It's called "Crisis in command." I remember because we had to study at the military academy. It mentions, for example, this aspect where they said it is an error to replace constituent units, companies, battalions, one unit by the other. It's much better to replace individuals when they have done their time on the battlefield or when the mobilisation is finished. The very last element of my reply is that in the course of the preparation of my report, I came across an order by General Ojdanic, which deals with the Kosovo situation in April 1999, where they talk about the incorporation of volunteers into the VJ during the Kosovo crisis and the NATO bombing, and in that order Ojdanic, who is the chief General Staff of the VJ explicitly prohibits the inclusion of volunteer units because he mentions there have been problems, looting, other crimes with units in the past. So I mean very long answer to, yeah, to show there's a huge difference between individual volunteers and volunteer units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, it would seem to me that as long as you have a difference in the mission of units taking part in armed conflict you would have trouble and problems arising out of that difference. The Presiding Judge asked you this morning exactly the same question, namely, and I'm merely just repeating the President's question, how was this transformed into the cooperation between the various units that took part in the armed conflict? I mean, if -- if what you're telling us is correct, namely that the JNA professional forces would work with the mission that was about brotherhood and unity and the volunteers of various groups would come with an ethnic mission, then my suggestion would be trouble is going to come out of that. So either the ethnic missions were transformed into a battle to secure territory, or the JNA would assume the political ethnic purpose that was carried by the volunteer groups. But can you revert to your answer to the President's question? How did this work out in practice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, in -- in practice there were, of course, problems, but I think that the length of the volume of reports also shows how complex the matter is, because, for example, the mission changes, the mission of the JNA, based on documents I reviewed. The mission in Croatia changes from the constitutional mission to a mission which is -- consists of, as is qualified by Kadijevic, protecting the Serbs which could be considered an ethnical mission. However -- and I think I can explain that best with a practical example, Vukovar. I know at least of one or even two non-Serb officers, I think they were of Macedonian ethnicity who had, for example, their name changed or they wanted to use another name during the conflict because they feared that the volunteers who were fighting along them would not trust them because Macedonian name it ended on "ovski" and it had to end on "ic," for example. This is a very small example but to show how this very, maybe, stratospheric level of brotherhood and unity, yeah, brotherhood and unity and ethnic we go down to what is happening in the field. In Vukovar there is no doubt based on the documents I reviewed that the volunteers, in particular the members of Leva Supoderica, were there to fight Ustashas. I'm quoting the vocabulary that is being used in articles that are from Velika Srbija that are kind of glorifying the activity of Leva Supoderica. There were still JNA officers in the Guards Brigade and other units who believed that they were fighting to maintain the unity of Yugoslavia. Whether that belief was correct or incorrect I think that's another question, but to summarise the situation was indeed complex. There were sometimes conflicts between -- on the field between the lowest level command and his JNA soldiers on one hand and the volunteers he was in command of because they were not always doing the same. Maybe they were willing to fight, to continue and take the next street or next group of houses in Vukovar, but there were also situations where they didn't feel like fighting. Why that was that could be related to the different motivation, the underlying motivation which is different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. We're going to stop here. It was starting to be really interesting, but we have to stop because of time constraints. Witness, you've taken the solemn declaration. You're now a Chamber's witness. You're an expert witness, and you're impartial. Furthermore, you are under oath now, and -- but you are a staff member of the OTP. Obviously you can continue working at the OTP, but you are absolutely not allowed to speak to anyone about your current testimony. As a military man, you know what this implies. So you're not to mention your testimony to anyone. You can talk about the weather, about the next football match or whatever, but not about the case. Did you get me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And if I may interject, Your Honour, and reassure Your Honours the chief of prosecutions Mr. Gavin Ruxton has instructed Mr. Theunens not to come to work while his testimony is ongoing and not to have any contact with any member of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you're on leave, actually. It's even better. Really lucky.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, this is an oral decision lifting the confidentiality. Noting the request of yesterday to lift the confidentiality of the transcript from page 3551, line 9 to page 3553, line 7 regarding the -- after -- regarding deliberation of the Chamber regarding orphans that would have been handed over to the opposing party during World War II, given that all this -- that most of this is already public information decides to lift the confidentiality of this part of the transcript, which means that pages 3551 to 3553 are now in the public domain. This was my ruling. We will meet next week for a hearing on Tuesday at 9.00 a.m. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 19th day of February, 2008, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.25 p.m.,
